Hubble Space Telescope. A space-based optical observatory launched by NASA in nineteen-ninety and deployed by the Space Shuttle program, orbiting Earth at an altitude of roughly five hundred seventy kilometers. Originally crippled by a spherical aberration in its primary mirror, it was repaired by astronauts in nineteen-ninety-three and has since become one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built. It revolutionized our understanding of the universe's age, expansion rate, and the prevalence of planets around other stars. Its longevity and continuous servicing by shuttle missions demonstrate the viability of space-based astronomy and human spaceflight for scientific discovery.

Launched in nineteen-ninety as the flagship of NASA's Great Observatories program, the telescope suffered from spherical aberration that severely blurred initial images. It's named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, who discovered the expansion of the universe and measured galaxy distances in the nineteen-twenties. Space shuttle astronauts repaired it in December nineteen-ninety-three when corrective optics were installed, restoring the telescope to full clarity.

Hubble observed the first definitive evidence of black holes at galactic centers and measured the supermassive black hole in Andromeda. It determined the Hubble Constant more precisely by observing Cepheid variable stars in distant galaxies, refining estimates of the universe's age. The telescope detected the acceleration of cosmic expansion, attributed to dark energy, leading to the nineteen-ninety-eight Nobel Prize in Physics discoveries.

The Hubble Deep Field image from nineteen-ninety-five revealed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky, becoming an iconic observation. The telescope was serviced five times by space shuttle astronauts between nineteen-ninety-three and two-thousand-nine, installing new instruments and replacing degraded components.

Operating at ultraviolet and visible wavelengths, Hubble cannot observe infrared radiation like its successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, but remains crucial for optical observations and as a calibration standard for modern astronomy. The nineteen-ninety-eight Nobel Prize in Physics recognized Hubble observations showing the universe's accelerating expansion, revealing the existence of dark energy comprising most of the universe's mass-energy content. The space shuttle program was the vehicle that deployed and repeatedly serviced the telescope in orbit. NASA is the space agency that managed the Hubble program and continues to operate it.
